  <script type="application/ld+json">
  {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "FAQPage",
    "mainEntity": [
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "What is visual storytelling and why does it matter?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "Visual storytelling is using images, composition, and visual choices to tell a story instead of relying on words. It matters because people scroll fast. If your image can make someone stop and feel something in half a second, you've already won the hardest part of content creation. My image-only posts consistently outperform my text-heavy ones in every engagement metric I track."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "How do I create visual hierarchy in my images?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "Think about what you want the person to see first, and make that the biggest, brightest, or most colorful thing in the frame. Everything else should support it, not compete with it. A simple test: squint at your image until it goes blurry. Can you still tell what the main subject is? If not, strip it back. In Western cultures, people tend to look at the upper left first."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "Should I use single images or carousels for visual storytelling?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "It depends on whether your story has one beat or several. Single images work best for one clear feeling or idea. Carousels are better for processes, transformations, before-and-afters, and anything that unfolds over time. On Instagram, carousels have consistently generated higher engagement in my experience, and the Socialinsider data backs this up. My rule: if you can't explain the story in one sentence, it probably needs multiple slides."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "How do I know if my visual storytelling is effective?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "Look at saves first. Saves mean someone thought your content was worth coming back to, which is a much stronger signal than a like. Then read the comments: are people describing the feeling you were going for, or are they just being polite? If your metrics are flat and your comments are generic, revisit your composition. Something probably isn't clear enough."
        }
      }
    ]
  }
